narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—signaled to the model that you would likely struggle on the bar. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. At 27, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted.

Other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 3.20, middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played much smaller roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Targeted bar-prep courses or additional study time could also help demonstrate readiness for the exam. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
